articles.description:
Akmal is a student of international relations and politics who has started a journey in geopolitics and international economics, and recently, political and social data science. Akmal has a history of extracurricular and volunteer activities, and I have learnt many transferable skills, including teamwork and discipline, that can be utilised in the workplace.
Outside of university and work, Akmal likes Star Wars and character illustration.

articles.title: Societal Determinism: How do Mothers have an Influence on a Child's IQ?
articles.contents:
By: Akmal G on November 4th, 2025
For one of my first works while learning from the University of Essex, I created a visualization that shows how a mother’s education, IQ and work status combined to influence children’ test scores. The visualization revealed a number of patterns of advantages and disadvantages across different family backgrounds.
The kidiq data stems from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth and is used in Gelman and Hill (2007). The data set contains 434 observations measured on five variables, and is obtained from https: //github.com/jknowles/BDAexampleR.data
I used the packages tidyverse, stringr, readr, ggplot2 and curl.


knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(curl)


My approach was to create categories that combine mother’s education and work status. Then, I processed child outcomes vary across these combined categories.


# Download and mutate data
kidiq.raw <- read_csv("kidiq-2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
kidiq <- kidiq.raw %>%
mutate(
  
# Create work status labels
work_status = case_when(
mom_work == 1 ~ "Not working",
mom_work == 2 ~ "Part-time",
mom_work == 3 ~ "Full-time",
mom_work == 4 ~ "Full-time+"
),
# Create highschool diploma success groups
highschool_diploma = case_when(
mom_hs == 0 ~ "High School Diploma",
mom_hs == 1 ~ "No High School Diploma",
),
# Create combined advantage categories
family_advantage = case_when(
mom_hs == 0 & mom_work <= 2 ~ "Low",
mom_hs == 0 & mom_work > 2 ~ "Mixed",
mom_hs == 1 & mom_work <= 2 ~ "Mixed",
mom_hs == 1 & mom_work > 2 ~ "High",
),
# Create age groups
age_group = case_when(
mom_age >= 17 & mom_age <= 20 ~ "Ages 17-20",
mom_age >= 21 & mom_age <= 23 ~ "Ages 21-23",
mom_age >= 24 & mom_age <= 26 ~ "Ages 24-26",
mom_age >= 27 & mom_age <= 29 ~ "Ages 27-29"
),
# Create IQ terciles for grouping
iq_group = case_when(
mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.33, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Lower IQ",
mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.67, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Middle IQ",
TRUE ~ "Higher IQ"
)
)

kidiq$age_group <- factor(kidiq$age_group, labels = c(
"Ages 17-20","Ages 21-23", "Ages 24-26","Ages 27-29"))
kidiq$iq_group <- factor(kidiq$iq_group, labels = c(
"Lower IQ", "Middle IQ", "Higher IQ"))
kidiq$work_status <- factor(kidiq$work_status, labels = c(
"Not working", "Part-time", "Full-time","Full-time+"))
kidiq$family_advantage <- factor(kidiq$family_advantage, labels = c(
"Low", "Mixed", "High"))
kidiq <- as.data.frame(kidiq)


To indicate different effects on IQ, I added additional dimensions using different colors, size, and faceting to differentiate. In the end, I was able to tell a story about social mobility and opportunity through a readable violin plot.


k1 <- ggplot(kidiq, aes(x = family_advantage, y = kid_score, color = age_group)) +
geom_violin() +
facet_wrap(~age_group) +
scale_color_brewer(palette = "RdPu") +
labs(
title = "Family Ties? Does a mother’s educational and employment
background affect their child's performance",
subtitle = "Correlation between family advantage with child's",
x = "Mother's Household Advantage",
y = "Child's Test Score",
caption = "Data: Test scores and mother's characteristics") +
theme_minimal()
print(k1)



The correlation between a mother’s educational and employment background, collectively known as Family Advantage, and the academic performance of their children is shown across several age groups. Most data seems to be sporadic,with notable exceptions being unemployed and full-time working mothers in the age range 24-26, and unemployed mothers in their late teens, having children who reached the mode performance scores.

articles.title: Electoral Turnout in the UK
articles.contents:
By: Akmal G on November 4th, 2025
For this project, I created a visualization that shows how electoral turnouts differ between the UK, Scotland, Ireland and Wales, from a very complicated dataset.
Step 1 - Load Packages
Firstly, I download several packages. Installing the “stringr” package allows for manipulate characters, use whitespace, and match patterns between function. I also install the “readr” package that allows us to read rectangular data (i.e. CSV and TSV) from delimited files, and the “ggplot2” package allows us to produce statistical data and graphics.
THere are also additional packages I need to doanload for readibility; the “curl” package provides bindings to the libcurl C library, while “tidyverse” package allows our data and graphs to be presented in a more presentable fashion.


library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(curl)


Step 2 - Raw data filtration
First, I place the election result data from the website into object uk_csv. I place the read data from the website and removing column names from the previous object into a new object, uk_raw.I then replace all unreadable data with \s+ with readable underscores, I recheck all data using ‘print’ before moving on.


uk_csv <- "https://electionresults.parliament.uk/general-elections/6/candidacies.csv"
uk_raw <- readr::read_csv(uk_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
names(uk_raw) <- names(uk_raw) %>% tolower() %>% str_replace_all("\\s+", "_")
print(uk_csv)

print(uk_raw)

Step 3 - Refine data to only elections
Now that I have the relevant object, I then filter the column of election_is_by-election, then I select certain columns relating only to constituency, country, valid votes and electorate. Then, rename these columns.

uk2 <- uk1 %>%
  select(
    constituency = constituency_name,
    country      = country_name,
    valid_votes  = candidate_vote_count,
    electorate   = electorate
  )

Step 4 — Calculate turnout percentages
I create a new data frame, grouping all constituncies data by their respective countries, and remove all missing data. Using the mutate function, I calculate the percentage of turnout registered, by dividing the data of valid votes over electorates. I then take a summarized glimpse into the the new data set.


uk3 <- uk2 %>%
  group_by(country, constituency) %>%
  summarise(
    valid_votes = sum(valid_votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    electorate  = max(electorate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
uk3

# A tibble: 650 × 4
   country constituency             valid_votes electorate
   <chr>   <chr>                          <dbl>      <dbl>

uk <- uk3 %>%
  mutate(turnout_registered = 100 * valid_votes / electorate) %>%
  filter(is.finite(turnout_registered), electorate > 0)
glimpse(uk)

$ turnout_registered <dbl> 61.79777, 58.22280, 69.50625, 59.44567, 7…

Now we have a list of constituencies with their turnout rates, we look up the top and bottom turnout constituencies. These two lines of code look quite similar; this is the function uk %>% doing its work, the function to mutate.
Step 5 — Data Wrangling, Organisation and pattern Recognition
Sort out the constituencies with the highest turnouts registered, and the lowest, into objects.
For the 10 highest-turnout places, all electorates seem to come from England and have an average voter turnout of 72%; Harpenden and Berkhamsted being the highest.
For the 10 lowest-turnout places, the have an average voter turnout is around 40 to 43.
For the 25 highest-turnout places, with a larger range of data, the average voter turnout is around 70 to 75%.
For the 25 lowest-turnout places, the average voter turnout is around 39 to 47%.
For the low-turnout polities, I noticed that only half of the valid population voted. On the other hand, third-quarter of the population voted in the polities with the highest turnout rates. The conclusion seems to be that a greater sample and range allows for a greater range and mode.

bottom10 <- uk %>% arrange(turnout_registered) %>% slice_head(n = 10)

Step 6 - Investigate Turnout
We now print out the turnoutrat by Constituent Countries of the UK. ‘n’ indicates the number of sample constituencies from each country (e.g. there are 543 sample constituncies from England). It is important to know the number of samples in a country to ensure the workings behind the mean and median turnout. I then create country summary (mean, median, n), ordered by mean turnout, and compile it into an object.


turnout_by_country <- uk %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_turnout   = mean(turnout_registered, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_turnout = median(turnout_registered, na.rm = TRUE),
    n              = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_turnout))
print(turnout_by_country)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  country          mean_turnout median_turnout     n
  <chr>                   <dbl>          <dbl> <int>
1 England                  60.1           60.7   543
2 Scotland                 59.2           58.6    57
3 Northern Ireland         57.1           58.2    18
4 Wales                    56.2           56.8    32

Step 7 - Visualisation of Findings
Using ggplot, I finally visualize the findings on turnout on each country. England shows the highest median turnout. One plausible reason for this is its large sample size of 543 constituencies …and hence a greater chance of finding a high turnout rate.
I added three changes to the visualization in order to improve it. I changed the bar width from 0.7 to 0.95, to improve visibility of the compatibility between the countries’ turnout. I changed the expansion multiplier from c(0, 0.05) to c(-0.5, -0.35), I added geom_text to add the turnout (y-value) of each country, so it magnifies the margin of difference between the turnout percentage between the y values of 50 and 65.
There were two failed approaches. I tried to change the geom_col into geom_line and geom_bar, but neither were interesting enough to look at. I tried to change the geom_col into geom_point, but there was not enough data and looked too simple. And stupid.
Improved Framework


ggplot(turnout_by_country, aes(country, mean_turnout, colours)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.95, fill = "#59c7d4") +  # bar = mean turnout
  geom_text(aes(label = signif(mean_turnout, digits = 3)), 
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), 
            vjust = -0.75, color = "black", size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(-0.5, -0.35))) +
  labs(
    title = "UK 2024 General Election: Mean Turnout by Country",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Turnout (% of registered voters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

articles.title: Sentiment Analysis of FOMC Bank Statements
articles.contents:
By: Akmal G on March 26th, 2026
In this project, I looked at the use of uncertainty language as well as output and inflation topics in a subsection of Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) statements made by the U.S. central bank. At the end, I also create an additional investigation on the role of energy in the wording of these statements and its confidence.
Applying dictionaries to FOMC policy statements
Because the file names actually have the date of the meeting, we are going to collect the filenames in an object.


library(quanteda)
library(readtext)
require(ggplot2)
filenames <- list.files("FOMC", "\\.txt$") # Import data


Extracting FOMCs from a list of files, I then read these texts using str.
I then turn their texts into a corpus.


txts <-  readtext(paste0("FOMC",  "/", "*.txt"))[]
str(txts)

Classes 'readtext' and 'data.frame':    96 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ doc_id: chr  "2005_02_1.txt" "2005_02_2.txt" "2005_02_3.txt" "2005_02_4.txt" ...
 $ text  : chr  "The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to raise its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis poin"| __truncated__ "The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to keep its target for the federal funds rate at 2 1$4 percent."| __truncated__ "The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to raise its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis poin"| __truncated__ "The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to raise its target for the federal funds rate by 50 basis poin"| __truncated__ ...

substring(texts(txts)["2005_02_1.txt"], 1, 150)

                                                                                                                                             2005_02_1.txt 
"The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to raise its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 2 1$4 percent. \n\nThe Committee be" 

txtCorpus <- corpus(txts)
head(summary(txtCorpus))

           Text Types Tokens Sentences
1 2005_02_1.txt   113    177         8

6 2005_03_2.txt   124    191         7

Then we might want to add in doc-level meta-info (Note that this was disabled in the current version (4.0.2


#metadoc(txtCorpus, "language") <- "english"
#metadoc(txtCorpus, "owner") <- "Akmal Gifari"
#metadoc(txtCorpus, "docsource")  <- paste("txts", 1:ndoc(txtCorpus))
#head(summary(txtCorpus, showmeta = TRUE))


Key Words in Context
To make sure that the statement has information about the economy and uncertainty, we might want to check using our KWIC command for the word ‘might’.


#key-words in context
options(width = 30)
might <- kwic(tokens(txtCorpus), "might")
head(might)

DFM
We then tokenize this text, using the functions tokens and dfm.


tokensFromCorp <- tokens(txtCorpus) 
dfmCorp <- dfm(tokensFromCorp)
topfeatures(dfmCorp, 20)

      the        to         .         ,       and inflation        in 
     1126       789       689       681       438       385       370 
       of committee    growth  economic      that   federal        be 
      338       285       236       235       216       194       162

      160       156       155       152       146       140 

Making a Dictionary
In order to show how to apply a dictionary, we import a dictionary which is already a list. In this case, we will use the uncertainty dictionary from the finance literature. We use this matrix to compare and contrast the frequency of specific and vague key terms.


test_dict <- dictionary(list(
  specific = c("clear*", "certain*", "unequi*"),
  vague = c("probably", "uncert*", "might", "could")))
precision <- dfm_lookup(dfmCorp, dictionary = test_dict)
tail(precision)

  consumerinflation = c("inflation", "price", "cost", "housing"), 
  output = c("growth", "gap", "employment", "output gap"),

I then turn our dictionary into a dictionary object, which will make the dfm using only the terms that appear in the dictionary. We build a new list of uncertainty words that start with the letter a and call this a `A uncertainty dictionary’.
‘A’ Uncertainty Dictionary


#read in dictionary - would need files of type YOSHIKODER
Uncertaintydict <- dictionary(list(uncertainty = c("abeyance",
"abeyances",
"almost",
"alteration",
"alterations",

Food for Thought: The Role of Energy
For an additional investigation, I substituted the above function of the dictionary for uncertain words, with one related to energy. I would like to investigate the effect of energy prices on the central banks’ statements.



I then repeat the process for dfm.


energyeffectdfm <- dfm_lookup(dfmCorp, dictionary = energyeffect, 
                         valuetype = "glob", case_insensitive = TRUE) 
head(energyeffectdfm)

Document-feature matrix of: 6 documents, 3 features (33.33% sparse) and 0 docvars.
               features
docs            energy consumerinflation vague
  2005_02_1.txt      1                 5     0
  2005_02_2.txt      1                 5     0
  2005_02_3.txt      1                 5     0
  2005_02_4.txt      1                 3     0
  2005_03_1.txt      1                 5     0
  2005_03_2.txt      1                 4     0

tail(energyeffectdfm)

Document-feature matrix of: 6 documents, 3 features (27.78% sparse) and 0 docvars.
               features
docs            energy consumerinflation vague
  2007_10_3.txt      0                 5     0
  2007_10_4.txt      1                 5     0
  2007_11_1.txt      1                 7     1
  2007_11_2.txt      1                 7     0
  2007_11_3.txt      1                 7     1
  2007_11_4.txt      1                 6     0

In addition, I visualize this using ggplot and tidyverse. First I turn it into a data frame and mutate the data using the ‘%>%’ function, summarising them all using pivot longer.


library(tidyverse)
dfm_counts_all <- convert(energyeffectdfm, to = "data.frame") %>%
  mutate(year = substr(doc_id, 1, 4)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    energy = sum(energy), 
    inflation = sum(consumerinflation),
    vagueness = sum(vague))

df_long <- dfm_counts_all %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(energy, inflation, vagueness), 
               names_to = "Metric", 
               values_to = "Count")


I then create the plot using a faceted ggplot. The plot shows an inversely proportional relationship between the role of the changes in energy prices and the level of vaguess and frequency of inflation discussion among the banks statements.


ggplot(df_long, aes(x = year, y = Count, color = Metric, group = Metric)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~Metric, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "energy" = "chartreuse4", 
    "inflation" = "sienna3", 
    "vagueness" = "maroon")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Comparing Trends Across Different Frequencies")

articles.title: Detecting Frequent Words in UK Manifestos
articles.contents:
By: Akmal G on March 26th, 2026
In this project, I looked at the use of diction and the frequency of certain words, in order to deduce speech patterns of UK politicians, using evidence from a corpus of manifestos.
I first load the following packages; quanteda, readtext, ggplot2, ggthemes and tidyverse.


library(quanteda)
library(readtext)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
library(tidyverse)


The argument docvarsfrom= allows us to use the file names as document ids; ‘> corpusSource object containing 69 texts of manifestos and 1 docvar’. We then need to turn the text files into a ‘corpus’, just to make sure the docnames are as expected (is being corrected in rebuild). Using ntoken and ntype, we can give names to the documents in question.


manifestos <- readtext("UK Manifestos/*.txt", docvarsfrom = c("filenames"))
manifestos #to check

readtext object consisting of 69 documents and 1 docvar.
# A data frame: 69 × 3
  doc_id      text                docvar1
  <chr>       <chr>               <chr>  
1 Con1918.txt "\"1918 Conse\"..." Con1918
2 Con1922.txt "\"1922 Conse\"..." Con1922
3 Con1923.txt "\"1923 Conse\"..." Con1923
4 Con1924.txt "\"1924 Conse\"..." Con1924
5 Con1929.txt "\"1929 Conse\"..." Con1929
6 Con1931.txt "\"1931 Conse\"..." Con1931
# ℹ 63 more rows

manifestos_corpus <- corpus(manifestos, docnames = manifestos$doc_id)

docnames(manifestos_corpus)

 [1] "Con1918.txt"  "Con1922.txt"  "Con1923.txt"  "Con1924.txt" 
 [5] "Con1929.txt"  "Con1931.txt"  "Con1935.txt"  "Con1945.txt" 
 [9] "Con1950.txt"  "Con1951.txt"  "Con1955.txt"  "Con1959.txt"

[21] "Con1992.txt"  "Con1997.txt"  "Con2001.txt"  "Lab1918.txt" 
[25] "Lab1922.txt"  "Lab1923.txt"  "Lab1924.txt"  "Lab1929.txt" 
[29] "Lab1931.txt"  "Lab1935.txt"  "Lab1945.txt"  "Lab1950.txt" 
[33] "Lab1951.txt"  "Lab1955.txt"  "Lab1959.txt"  "Lab1964.txt"

ntk <- ntoken(manifestos_corpus) # shows the tokens per document
ntps <- ntype(manifestos_corpus) # shows the types per document

# There are 562339 tokens per document and 121676 types per document.
sum(ntk)

[1] 562339

There is a difference between types and tokens.To summarize the corpus, for example, we may want to consider whether UK party manifestos getting longer or shorter over time. We can look at the number of sentences for each manifesto. I grabbed the dates of the manifestos, which could be done with docvars()<, but could also be done with regex.


num_sentences <- nsentence(manifestos_corpus)
num_sentences

head(Dates)

We notice from sum(num_sentences) that there 24524 words to look through.Then we plot them either in base scatterplot as well as a nicer ggplot.

head(info_summary)

            Dates Sentences

info_summary[69,]

  theme_hc()



Looking inside the Documents
To see this, lets grab the Labor 1983 manifesto alone, then we transform them into tokens. Simply using the length function counts the number of tokens to around 25000; using the unique funtion counts the number of unique tokens to around 3600


Lab_1983 <- corpus_subset(manifestos_corpus, docvar1=="Lab1983")
summary(Lab_1983)

Corpus consisting of 1 document, showing 1 document:

        Text Types Tokens Sentences docvar1
 Lab1983.txt  3673  25131      1108 Lab1983

tokens_all <- tokens(Lab_1983) #this defaults to the /word/ level
head(tokens_all)

Tokens consisting of 1 document and 1 docvar.
Lab1983.txt :
 [1] "Foreward" "Here"     "you"      "can"      "read"     "Labour's"
 [7] "plan"     "to"       "do"       "the"      "things"   "crying"  
[ ... and 25,119 more ]

length(tokens_all[[1]]) #~25k

[1] 25131

length(unique(tokens_all[[1]])) #~3.6k

[1] 3673

For grater clarity, we could remove punctuation and some numbers.
Note that your research question should drive this choice and length of your documents might play a role.
More Information: DennySpirling


# Check and remove punctuation tokens; then place it in an object.
tokens_nopunc <- tokens(Lab_1983, remove_punct=T)
length(tokens_nopunc[[1]]) #~22.5k

[1] 22513

# Check and remove punctuation tokens as well as numbers.
tokens_nopunc_nonum <- tokens(Lab_1983, remove_punct=T, remove_number=T)
length(tokens_nopunc_nonum[[1]]) #~22.4k

[1] 22396

It would help us to separated bi-grams (only) from a set of uni-grams and bi-grams.
While tokens_ngrams() generates n-grams or skip-grams in all possible combinations of tokens, tokens_compound() generates n-grams more selectively. Bi-grams can be negated using phrase() and a wild card (*).


toks_ngram <- tokens_ngrams(tokens_nopunc_nonum, n = 2)
head(toks_ngram[[1]], 20)

 [1] "Foreward_Here" "Here_you"      "you_can"       "can_read"     
 [5] "read_Labour's" "Labour's_plan" "plan_to"       "to_do"

[13] "out_to"        "to_be"         "be_done"       "done_in"      
[17] "in_our"        "our_country"   "country_today" "today_To"     

# Reveal the top part of the list of bi-grams.

toks_neg_bigram <- tokens_compound(tokens_nopunc_nonum, pattern = phrase("not *"))
head(toks_neg_bigram[[1]], 20)

 [1] "Foreward" "Here"     "you"      "can"      "read"     "Labour's"
 [7] "plan"     "to"       "do"       "the"      "things"   "crying"  
[13] "out"      "to"       "be"       "done"     "in"       "our"     
[19] "country"  "today"   

# Reveal the top part of the list of uni-grams - notice the lack of bi-grams.

toks_neg_bigram_select <- tokens_select(toks_neg_bigram, pattern = phrase("not_*"))
head(toks_neg_bigram_select[[1]], 20)

 [1] "not_just"         "not_counted"      "not_true"        
 [4] "not_be"           "not_true"         "not_be"

[10] "not_be"           "not_an"           "not_only"

[16] "not_undermined"   "not_however"      "not_be"          
[19] "not_create"       "not_allow"       

# Reveal the top part of the list of bi-grams with 'not' in front.


The material in Quanteda recommends using the tokens_compound command to get top tokens rather than the tokens_ngrams.
Stemming
Using the Porter Stemmer, I can see what package this is coming from an what stemmed it is using by doing ?tokens_wordstem. Stemming removes all words of the similar family, in this case, the word ‘family’.


stemmed <- tokens_wordstem(tokens_all) #can inspect directly, if desired.
# to see what's happened in practice, let's compare 'family' and 'families'.
# So, compare
tokens_all[[1]][grep("fam",tokens_all[[1]])]

# to
stemmed[[1]][grep("fam",stemmed[[1]])]

Stopwords
I would also like to remove the all stopwords, in English.


stopwords("english")

  [1] "i"          "me"         "my"         "myself"     "we"        
  [6] "our"        "ours"       "ourselves"  "you"        "your"

Vector Space Representation


Lab_1983 <- corpus_subset(manifestos_corpus, docvar1=="Lab1983")
Lab1983_vector <- tokens(Lab_1983)
# Categorize any words into any available tokens.
Lab1983_vector <- tokens_wordstem(Lab1983_vector)
# Categorize tokens into word steams
Lab1983_vector <- dfm(Lab1983_vector, tolower = TRUE)
# Transform data into readable matrix
head(Lab1983_vector)


With the following objects, I can make a dfm of the whole Manifestos collection, and give weight to the most common words in the corpus.


# Create object with all manifestos for past UK elections.
manifestos <- readtext("UK Manifestos/*.txt", docvarsfrom = c("filenames"))
manifestos <- corpus(manifestos)

# Remove all punctuation and English stopwords from each speech.
dfmat_man <- tokens(manifestos, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |>
  dfm()
dfmat_man

# Create an alternate weighted set using the frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf).
dfmat_man_weighted <- dfm_tfidf(dfmat_man)

# Compare and contrast dfmat_man and dfmat_man_weighted

environmental   environment        police      liberals         crime

           uk           new          tory          1979     standards 
     83.35082      82.80990      82.64681      82.04413      81.54135 

Visual Representation of Word Frequency
We can visualize this with ggplot’s bar graphs. It better shows the frequency of words in dfmat_man. We mutate the data for dfmat_man, then we visualize it. The object dfmat_man, on one hand, provides a sum of the frequency of certain keywords. This includes ‘government’, ‘new’, ‘people’, ‘must’, ‘can’ and ‘local’, which may initially indicate the frequency of how candidates tend to provide election promises at their incumbencies. The function dfmat_man_weighted, on the other hand, gives these words weight in comparison to their frequency among the whole group; judging on rare or frequent they may appear.
For dfmat_man;


top_raw <- topfeatures(dfmat_man, 20) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  rownames_to_column("word") %>% 
  rename(count = ".")

ggplot(top_raw, aes(x = reorder(word, count), y = count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "salmon") +
  coord_flip() + # Makes it a horizontal bar chart so words are readable
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Top 20 Most Frequent Words in UK Manifestors", x = NULL, y = "Raw Count")



For dfmat_man_weighted;


top_weighted <- topfeatures(dfmat_man_weighted, 20) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  rownames_to_column("word") %>% 
  rename(tfidf = ".")

ggplot(top_weighted, aes(x = reorder(word, tfidf), y = tfidf)) +
  geom_col(fill = "palevioletred") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Top 20 Most Unique Words, Mutated with TF-IDF", x = NULL, y = "TF-IDF Weight")
